title: One ummah, many faces
hookLine: Arab, Persian, Turkish, African, Malay, Chinese, European

cards: Friday, in a big-city mosque. The row forms, shoulder to shoulder. On the left, a taxi driver whose family came from Cairo.
Next to him a student from Istanbul, then a grandfather from Lagos, a nurse whose parents came from Kuala Lumpur, a man from Xi'an in a white cap, a convert from Sarajevo, an engineer from Tehran.
Different languages in the parking lot, different food at home, different ways of tying a headscarf or a turban. Then the imam says God is greatest, and every one of them raises their hands at once.

teach.b: Ummah is the Arabic word for a community, a people, and Muslims use it for the whole worldwide community of believers. First, the Qur'an names it as one.
In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! this, your religion, is one religion, and I am your Lord, so worship Me." Second, the many faces were there among the Prophet's own companions.

teach.h: BILAL, SALMAN, SUHAYB: A MIXED CIRCLE.
teach.b: Bilal, of Abyssinian descent, gave his voice to the call to prayer. Salman came from Persia, searching for the truth. Suhayb, who grew up among the Byzantines, was called the Roman.
The community around the Prophet, peace be upon him, was mixed before it was large. Third, the line that set the rule.

teach.h: NO ARAB ABOVE A NON-ARAB, EXCEPT BY PIETY.
teach.b: In the sermon of the Prophet's last pilgrimage, as Musnad Ahmad reports it, he said no Arab is above a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab above an Arab, nor a light-skinned person above a dark-skinned one, nor the other way, except by piety.
Rank by birth was cut off at the root. Fourth, what the history adds.
This path has walked through Arab caliphs, Persian poets, Turkish sultans, West African scholars, Malay sultanates, Chinese mosques and the old Muslims of the Balkans.
They prayed toward the same house in Mecca, in Arabic, then went home and cooked their own food, sang their own songs and built in their own style.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari pictures believers as one body: when one part aches, the whole body feels it.
One body, many faces. The history suggests that's a feature, not a problem to fix.

how: Muslims of every background pray in the same rows, facing the Ka'ba in Mecca and reciting in Arabic, while keeping their own languages, dress, food and festivals.

o: the Arab people, the Prophet's own
the worldwide community of believers, as one
the call that summons people to prayer

p: of Abyssinian descent; the call to prayer
from Persia, searching for the truth

s: the Prophet's companions were all Arabs
Bilal was of Abyssinian descent and Salman came from Persia; Suhayb, raised among the Byzantines, was called the Roman.
a hadith pictures believers as one body that feels when one part aches
being one ummah means every Muslim culture should look the same
the history shows one religion and one direction of prayer, with every land keeping its own food, songs and buildings.

games.q: you're preaching at the last pilgrimage, to a crowd from many tribes and peoples. what do you say about rank?
o: the Arabs, as first believers, rank highest.
no one is above another by birth or color, except by piety.
rank goes to those who came earliest.
games.why: Musnad Ahmad reports the Prophet saying no Arab is above a non-Arab, nor a light-skinned person above a dark-skinned one, nor the other way, except by piety.

practice: Choose the place from today you know least about, West Africa, Malaysia, China, Bosnia, Iran, Turkey, Egypt, and picture someone there right now at the same prayer, saying the same Arabic words in a room that looks nothing like yours.
What are they wearing, what does the street sound like, what will they eat after? If you pray, remember them in your next prayer.

wordCard.voice: One ummah. The worldwide community of Muslims: one religion, one direction of prayer, and every face, language and culture inside it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a community, a people; for Muslims, the worldwide community of believers.

carryVoice: Your line: many faces. One body, and every part feels the others. See you tomorrow.
